source.title: Training Optimal Large Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Jinjie Ni; Qian Liu; Chao Du; Long-Xu Dou; Hang Yan; Zi-Li Wang; Tian-Yu Pang; M. Shieh

record.file_problem: The text contains the full paper, including appendices. It identifies itself as an initial draft.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures loss and compute-optimal allocation using IsoFLOPs profiles and parametric loss fitting modeled on the cited scaling-law approach, applied to diffusion language models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own compute-constrained and data-constrained scaling results. Results from the schedule, loss-formula, batch-size, learning-rate, weight-decay and benchmark ablations are not recorded unless they bear on a listed scaling claim. The paper extrapolates optimal allocations, but does not report observed losses of runs orders of magnitude larger than the runs used for fitting.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Hoffmann et al. IsoFLOPs and parametric-fit methods to the same quantities (final pretraining loss, compute-optimal N and D) for diffusion language models. It reports its own allocation exponents and loss fits. It also fits a multi-epoch validation-loss law on repeated data. T3 (new model class) is also defensible.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly accurate. The authors also state that their data-constrained law reduces exactly to the Chinchilla form at one epoch, and that AR batch-size and learning-rate practices transfer to DLMs. They stress that scaling coefficients shift across architectures and datasets, so the laws are high-level guidance only.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IsoFLOPs profiles and parametric loss fitting based on the cited AR scaling-law methods, but applies them to diffusion language models and adds a data-constrained validation-loss model for repeated epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: The two compute-constrained approaches yield similar allocation exponents but different coefficients. The paper states that scaling-law coefficients can shift across architectures and datasets; the data-constrained fit can overshoot optimal epochs, underestimate model size, and miss some validation losses. It also smooths compute-constrained losses with a window of 301, which the authors say reduces variance by about 13× at the cost of a mild bias corresponding to about a 40-step lag.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted epoch at which overfitting begins scales with unique data and model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In repeated-data DLM training, the overfitting-onset epoch scales approximately as UD^0.39/N^0.55.

record.problems: The compute-constrained results fit final training loss, while the claim concerns held-out loss. The paper notes that the validation-loss form lacks a strict theoretical justification, that some long-epoch runs show double descent, and that fitted optima and validation losses can differ noticeably from actual results. The authors also state that validation-loss values depend heavily on the validation set and tokenizer.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's schedule, kernel, loss-formula, batch-size, learning-rate, weight-decay and downstream benchmark ablations were left out because they do not test the listed scaling-law versions. No observed large-run loss result was reported for the paper's extrapolated allocation estimates.

untested.parts: No observed loss of a run much larger than the fitting runs is compared with the fit; the LLaDA-budget and Table 2 allocations are projections only.
Table 6 lists configurations of varying depth and width, but shape is never varied at fixed N to test its effect on loss.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not studied; only repeated-data text pretraining is.
HellaSwag and MMLU are used only in design ablations at 1B scale, not as functions of scale or loss.
The compute-constrained fits use smoothed training loss (single epoch) rather than a separate held-out set. Loss as a direct function of compute along the frontier is shown only graphically (Fig. 3).

missing.what: Approach 1 and Approach 2 extrapolations diverge at large scale: at 10T parameters the token counts are 566.4T versus 1153.9T. The authors say the loss-fitting approach under-estimates N_opt for very large models, as in Hoffmann et al.

Alternative data-constrained formulas fit worse (fit loss 31.52 and 23.8 versus 9.78 over 23,145 points) and imply much smaller optimal models, about 100–280M in Fig. 18 versus about 0.5–4.6B in Fig. 5. The predicted allocation depends on the formula chosen.
The DLM irreducible loss E is 2.41 versus Chinchilla's 1.69; the authors attribute this to the ELBO objective.
Choice of a Gaussian smoothing window of 301 (versus 10 in Chinchilla), which reduces variance about 13× at a roughly 40-step lag. This is a fitting choice that could affect the coefficients.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T1 is chosen because the method and measure match Hoffmann et al.; the new model class (diffusion LMs) could justify T3. The paper is an initial-draft preprint. Compute-constrained runs use Nemotron-CC, while data-constrained runs use c4-en with c4-val validation. The reported run counts are inconsistent (21,345, about 24,000 and 23,145). No uncertainty estimates are reported for any exponent.

versions.untested_parts: The held-out validation-loss fit at one epoch is reported; the compute-constrained loss fit is to final training loss. The paper does not directly test held-out loss scaling with compute.
No comparison of small-run loss predictions with observed losses from runs orders of magnitude larger is reported.
The compute-optimal allocation is tested for the paper's DLM setup and compute range; the results do not establish the trend universally across model types or training setups.
Architecture configurations are listed, but depth, width or other architecture details are not varied to test their effect on loss at fixed parameter count.
Repeated-data training is examined. Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Downstream benchmark ablations are reported, but downstream performance is not tested for predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The paper reports differences between DLM and AR allocations, two DLM fitting approaches, and departures from a single-descent fit. It does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions or all training-schedule, data and fitting choices.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Runs span under 7M to over 11B parameters in the compute-constrained experiments; data-constrained fit uses 23,145 runs.
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a function of parameters, unique tokens and epochs; at one epoch the authors state that the formula reduces to a parameter-and-token loss law.
rows.measure: Fitted validation-loss relationship at one epoch
rows.value: At e ≤ 1, the authors state the fit reduces to L = 1535.23/N^0.42 + 54.21/UD^0.40.
rows.note: This is a fitted validation-loss relationship, not a direct test of held-out loss scaling with compute. The irreducible-loss term is omitted in the reported fitted form.
rows.check: The e ≤ 1 form follows algebraically from Eq. 15, which was fitted mostly to multi-epoch c4 runs; it is not a separate fit to single-epoch data. The power-law form is imposed, and the authors report noticeable fit gaps (R8). Run counts in the text are inconsistent: 21,345 (intro), about 24,000 (§4.1) and 23,145 (§4.2).

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Model sizes up to 11B parameters; datasets up to 260B tokens.
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model sizes at nine fixed FLOPs budgets, fit parabolas to IsoFLOPs loss profiles, and fit compute to the loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
rows.measure: Power-law exponents for compute-optimal parameter and token allocations
rows.value: Nopt ∝ C^a, Dopt ∝ C^b; a = 0.51 and b = 0.49. Fitted formulas: N ≈ 0.0216C^0.514 and D ≈ 7.7C^0.486.
rows.note: The reported fits show near-equal growth of the optimal parameter and token counts over the tested compute range.
rows.check: Fine. The fit is to smoothed final training loss of single-epoch runs, smoothed with a Gaussian window of 301.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a parametric loss function to final training losses and derive the fixed-compute allocation.

conditions.value: Huber loss on log-losses; L-BFGS; grid search over initial values

rows.measure: Fitted loss and compute-optimal allocation exponents
rows.note: The allocation exponents agree with the IsoFLOPs approach, while the fitted coefficients differ.
rows.check: Should also link to V1. The parametric fit L = 2.413 + 798.6/N^0.379 + 4604.9/D^0.378 is a power-law loss surface in N and D over runs from under 7M to over 11B parameters. For V7, its kN and kD (0.04 and 4.10) differ from Approach 1 (0.02 and 7.70) although the exponents match.

source_check.correct: The fitted response is final training loss: L(N,D) ≈ 2.413 + 798.6/N^0.379 + 4604.9/D^0.378. Table 1 gives a=b=0.50, kN=0.04 and kD=4.10. State: observed for V3 and V7; cannot_determine for V1, which specifies held-out pretraining loss.
source_check.problem: The observed state does not apply to V1: the fitted training-loss measure does not establish held-out loss scaling.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM scaling-law allocation (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted compute-optimal allocation coefficients with the Chinchilla allocations reported in the paper.

conditions.value: Quokka DLMs versus Chinchilla AR models
Quokka approaches 1 and 2; Chinchilla approaches 1 and 2 for allocation coefficients

rows.measure: Optimal token allocation at fixed compute
rows.value: Quokka has a 2.2–6.7× larger kD than Chinchilla; the paper also describes DLMs as requiring roughly 2–5× more tokens at the same FLOPs.
rows.note: The Chinchilla values are comparison values reported from prior work, not new Chinchilla experiments in this study.
rows.check: The Chinchilla coefficients are cited, not re-run. The row records a difference in the allocation multiplier (kD), not in the exponent, so it bears on V7 (setup and objective dependence) rather than V3, which is about the growth exponents.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Suite spans varying model sizes and unique-data budgets; the paper describes about 24,000 runs and fits 23,145 runs.
rows.operation_detail: Measure validation loss across model size, unique-data budget and training epochs.
rows.value: The authors report that validation loss eventually rises with sufficiently many epochs for any model size and unique-data budget; the loss is generally U-shaped, with a minority of runs showing double descent.
rows.note: This result concerns repeated-data training, where the loss does not remain a monotonically falling single power law.
rows.check: Loss first falls with epochs, then rises ('eventually increases'), so the effect is not reversed throughout. The decreasing phase is still captured by the authors' power-law-based effective-data form.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the epoch of overfitting onset as a function of unique data size and parameter count.

conditions.value: unique tokens UD and parameters N

rows.note: This is a power-law relationship for the overfitting-onset epoch, rather than a direct measure of the loss law or the fixed-compute allocation.
rows.check: This concerns the onset of overfitting, not a listed version. Keep under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare observed data-constrained validation-loss curves with the assumed single-descent fitted formulation.

conditions.value: A small subset of long-epoch runs

rows.measure: Departure from the fitted single-descent curve
rows.value: The authors report double-descent behavior in a small subset of long-epoch runs.
rows.note: The authors state that their fitting procedure truncates the second peak in these cases.
rows.check: Fine. No number is given for how many runs show double descent; the text says only 'a small subset'.

rows.subject: Quokka DLM training runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted data-constrained optima and validation-loss predictions with actual runs.

conditions.value: Fitted predictions versus actual optima and losses
Randomly sampled (N, UD, e) for loss comparison

rows.measure: Fit accuracy for optimal epochs, model sizes and validation losses
rows.value: The fitted contours tend to overshoot epochs and underestimate model size; the authors also report noticeable gaps between predicted and actual validation losses in some cases.
rows.note: The authors say Equation 15 captures the overall loss shape but that some predictions remain inaccurate.
rows.check: As evidence that the fitted curve departs from the data, the effect is observed, not partial. The predictions are within the fitted range, so this is not a V2 extrapolation test.

relationships.condition: Single-epoch DLM pretraining, under 7M to over 11B parameters and 1B to over 260B tokens
relationships.reason: The parametric fit gives power-law terms in N and D (exponents about 0.38), and the e≤1 reduction of Eq. 15 has the same form (R3, R1). The power-law form is imposed, not tested against alternatives.
relationships.display_finding: The adopted power-law form fitted training loss with parameter and data exponents around 0.38, matching the validation model's single-epoch reduction.
